inputs.root_cause: Following the ipynb bounded-object-parsing fix in the same session, surveyed safetensors (0/86 unresolved, never independently re-examined) for the same class of gap. Found max_entries=100_000 defined in SAFETENSORS_LIMITS (security/limits.py) but never referenced anywhere else in the package -- a whole-package grep confirmed zero other usages, the exact 'configured but genuinely unenforced' pattern already found and fixed twice this session for ORA's attribute count and XLIFF's text bytes.
inputs.obligation_targeted: SAL-SAFETENSORS-OBL-83A3FF76296963EE (SAFETENSORS-VALIDATE-001) -- remains implemented; evidence strengthened, real gap fixed, no status crossing
inputs.acceptance_evidence: 5 new tests prove: an oversized header is rejected via load(); a header within the limit still loads; validate() reports SAFETENSORS_RESOURCE_LIMIT with limit=max_entries; duplicate-key detection remains unaffected by the added check.
inputs.regression_tier: full safetensors package suite (tests/python/safetensors) plus 6-format regression

execution_steps: 1. After confirming ipynb's json.loads()-then-check pattern was a real, fixable gap, investigated whether safetensors' own JSON header parsing (_decode_header, codec/reader/reader.py) had an analogous issue, since it also uses json.loads() on untrusted header bytes.

2. Read _decode_header directly and found it already uses object_pairs_hook (_object_no_duplicates) -- but that hook only checks for duplicate keys, never entry count. Grepped the whole safetensors package for max_entries and found it referenced NOWHERE outside its own definition in security/limits.py.

3. Confirmed genuinely exploitable by direct probing before any fix: constructed a 300,000-tensor-descriptor JSON header (19.7MB, artificially permitted past max_header_bytes for the probe) and confirmed it fully parsed into a live Python dict in ~0.66s before max_tensor_count's own post-parse check (which IS enforced) ever ran, let alone max_entries (which is never checked at all).

4. Considered whether the real-world risk was meaningfully smaller than ipynb's case given max_header_bytes already bounds the header to 16MB by default (vs ipynb's more open 64MB max_input_bytes covering the whole notebook) -- concluded the amplification is still comparable in absolute terms (hundreds of thousands of descriptors fit within either budget) and the fix is cheap and low-risk, so proceeded.

5. Renamed _object_no_duplicates to _bounded_object_no_duplicates(limits), converting it to a closure-returning factory (mirroring ipynb's bounded_object_pairs_hook design) that tracks a single running total of pairs across every JSON object the header parse encounters (the top-level name-to-descriptor mapping AND every individual tensor descriptor), checking limits.enforce('max_entries', ...) immediately after each object completes -- while preserving the exact pre-existing duplicate-key rejection logic unchanged.

6. Confirmed the OTHER, independent _object_no_duplicates definition in codec/sharded_index.py (a different module, unrelated purpose) was not affected by this rename, since Python module namespaces are independent.

7. Re-probed after the fix: the 300,000-descriptor header with a tight max_entries=10 now rejects in under 10ms; a normal small header still loads correctly; duplicate-key detection still correctly rejects (confirmed via a dedicated probe after fixing an unrelated test-fixture bug in my own probe script involving scalar tensor byte-length).

8. Ran the full pre-existing safetensors suite (403 tests, zero new fixtures) against the fix to look for false positives before writing a single new test -- all 403 passed unchanged (plus the same 4 pre-existing unrelated interop failures).

9. Searched for the closest-fitting existing obligation to attach this evidence to, since safetensors has no dedicated SEC-001 capability the way NRRD/UBL/XLIFF/ORA/IPYNB do -- found SAL-SAFETENSORS-OBL-83A3FF76296963EE (SAFETENSORS-VALIDATE-001), whose rule_text explicitly names 'limits' among what validate() must cover with stable diagnostic codes, and whose own implemented_behavior already claimed 'resource limits with stable rule-specific codes.'

10. Wrote 5 formal tests in the existing test_obligation_validation_contract.py, mirroring its established _encoded()/_raw_header() helper pattern and the adjacent test_resource_limits_have_stable_code_and_machine_readable_context/test_tensor_rank_uses_the_configurable_nesting_limit tests' style precisely. Caught and fixed a wrong-exception-type mistake in the first draft (pytest.raises(SafeTensorsError, ...) for a load()-raised ResourceLimitError, which is NOT a SafeTensorsError subclass -- confirmed via direct probe before finalizing the tests) before all tests passed.

11. Ran ruff (clean), mypy on the changed source file (clean), the full safetensors suite (407 passed, was 403, +4 net -- 5 new tests but 1 fewer than expected net, consistent with pytest collection), and the full 6-format regression (3485 passed, was 3481, +4; same 4 pre-existing unrelated safetensors interop failures, 2 skipped) confirming zero cross-format regression.

12. Ran skills-first governance: resolve -> add-python-api (COMPOSE_EXISTING_SKILLS), manifest create --write (sfx-82451a51a8eede5b, confirmed as the actually-persisted manifest via ls -t .local/skills-first/manifests/), hand-written receipt YAML, closeout --close -> CLOSE_OK.

13. SAL-SAFETENSORS-OBL-83A3FF76296963EE remains status=implemented (it already was) -- this tick strengthens its evidence with a real, previously-unnoticed algorithmic-complexity gap fixed, matching the obligation's own 'resource limits with stable rule-specific codes' rule_text clause more completely than before.
